transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

Well, it’s... it’s kind of embarrassing, honestly, but I’m here because I’ve started planning my entire day, like, my whole schedule, around not using elevators. It sounds so silly when I say it out loud, but it’s just gotten to the point where it’s really messing with things. Like, I live on the fifth floor, right? And I’ve just been taking the stairs every single time. Five flights, up and down, even when I’m carrying groceries or coming home exhausted from work. I mean, the exercise is fine, I guess, but it’s not really about the exercise. 

And it’s starting to affect my job, too. I’m a training specialist, and I actually turned down leading this really great workshop last week just because it was going to be held on the 22nd floor of this high-rise downtown, and I just couldn't stomach the idea of getting in the elevator to go all the way up there. I made up some excuse about a scheduling conflict, but it was totally because of the elevator. I even had to stop doing home visits with one of my older computer students. He’s this really nice guy, but he lives in a building where the stairs are for emergencies only, and the only real way up to his apartment is the elevator. I just... I couldn't do it anymore. So, yeah, I guess I’m just avoiding them completely now, and it’s getting exhausting trying to work around it.

When you think about elevators or find yourself in situations where you might have to use one, do you experience persistent, unwanted thoughts that cause you a lot of anxiety, or feel like you have to do something over and over again to reduce that anxiety?

No, it's not really like that. I mean, I don't have thoughts just popping into my head out of nowhere, and I definitely don't do things over and over again. Like, I know some people have to, I don't know, check their locks ten times before they leave the house or wash their hands a bunch of times because they feel like they absolutely have to in order to calm down, and I don't have anything like that going on. My brain doesn't force me to do weird routines or anything. 

It’s strictly just... the elevator. Like, if I know I have a meeting or a training session at a new building, the only thought I have is, "Oh man, I really hope there are stairs I can use," and if I actually have to stand there and look at the elevator doors, I just get this really intense dread about getting stuck in there. You know, like the power failing and just being trapped in a tiny metal box for hours with no air. That's what I'm thinking about. But once I find the stairs and start walking, I'm totally fine. I don't have to count the steps or take them two at a time or do any sort of special ritual to make the anxiety go away. The anxiety goes away simply because I'm not getting in the elevator. So, yeah, no repetitive stuff or unwanted thoughts like you're saying, just... just thinking about how much I really, really don't want to get in that box.

When you think about getting into an elevator, do you ever experience sudden physical symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, trembling, or a feeling of shortness of breath, like you're having a panic attack?

Yeah, exactly that. It’s honestly like my body just completely takes over before my brain can even catch up. I mean, it’s not even a slow build-up where I’m standing there pondering whether or not I should get in. It’s so fast. Like, as soon as I even step toward an elevator, or if I’m just walking through a lobby and I hear it make that heavy, mechanical clunk when the doors open, my chest just instantly tightens up. It feels like someone pulled a belt around my ribs and yanked it tight. 

And my hands get incredibly sweaty, like instantly clammy, which is super annoying, especially if I'm holding training materials or my tablet for work. I just get this massive rush of panic before I’ve even had time to logically think it through. It’s wild because, you know, logically I know I’m just standing in a hallway, but my body is acting like I’m about to step off a cliff. My heart just starts hammering, and I get that shortness of breath you mentioned, where it feels like I can't quite get a full gulp of air. 

I remember this one time recently, I was at my buddy's apartment complex—he lives in this older building where the elevator makes this awful, echoing grinding noise—and just standing in the hallway waiting for him, looking at those closed metal doors, I started sweating right through my shirt. I was trembling so much I had to put my hands in my pockets so nobody would notice, and I eventually had to text him to just meet me outside because I couldn't stand there for another second. So, yeah, it’s a very intense, very sudden physical reaction. It’s like a complete system override, just boom, full panic, just from hearing the doors open.

Do you experience the same kind of intense physical reaction in other situations, like being in crowded places, open spaces, or when you’re outside your home alone, or is this panic strictly limited to elevators?

No, no, it's really just the elevators. I mean, I'm totally fine in crowds. Like, I go to concerts all the time, or I used to, before my schedule got so crazy with work. I love being down in the pit with hundreds of people all packed together, sweating and jumping around. It doesn't bother me at all. And open spaces? Pfft, I grew up going camping out west with my dad, wide open plains, huge skies, never felt an ounce of panic. I love being outside. 

And being outside my home alone isn't a problem either. I mean, I walk to the grocery store by myself, I take the subway—which, I know, is underground and kind of enclosed, but for some reason, the subway doesn't bother me. Maybe because it's bigger? Or because there are other people? I don't know. But I take the train all over the city by myself, no problem. I even go for runs in the park at night, just me and my headphones, and I feel completely safe and calm. 

It's literally just... that specific situation. The elevator. It's like my brain has just decided that this one particular invention is a death trap. I can be in a crowded room, totally fine. I can be in a tiny bathroom stall, totally fine. But you put me in a lobby looking at those sliding metal doors, and my heart just loses its mind. It's so weird how specific it is, you know? Like, why elevators? Why not closets or cars? I drive a tiny little compact car and I'm perfectly happy in there. But yeah, to answer your question, no, I don't get that panic anywhere else. Just the elevators. It's really frustrating because if it were just, like, a general fear of small spaces, I feel like it would make more sense. But it's just this one very specific thing that I have to deal with every single day.
Have you ever avoided other places or situations that make you feel like you could be trapped, like crowded subways, movie theaters, or long tunnels, even if you're not in an elevator?

No, not really. I mean, like I said about the subway, I'm totally fine on there. Even when it's rush hour and people are practically sitting on my lap, it doesn't bother me. I just put my headphones in, listen to a podcast, and tune it all out. And movie theaters? I love going to the movies. I'm one of those people who actually prefers to sit right in the middle of the row, surrounded by people, because I think the sound is better there. I don't get that feeling of needing to escape or being trapped at all. Even if someone tall sits in front of me or if I have to squeeze past a dozen knees to go to the bathroom, I never get that panic. 

And tunnels, no, not an issue. There's this really long tunnel on my drive to visit my parents, and sometimes traffic backs up right in the middle of it. You'd think that would be prime territory for feeling trapped, right? Just sitting there in a concrete tube under a mountain with nowhere to go. But honestly, I just turn up the radio and wait it out. I don't feel that chest-tightening, heart-racing thing. 

It really always comes back to just the elevator. It’s like my brain has a very specific file labeled "Danger," and the only thing in that file is an elevator. If I'm in a crowded theater or a tunnel or whatever, my brain just files that under "Normal Daily Annoyances" or "Fun Activities." But the second an elevator is involved, it's like a siren goes off. I remember my friend tried to tell me once that an elevator is basically just a vertical subway car, but I was like, "No, absolutely not, they are completely different." In a subway, there are doors at every car, there are windows, there's a conductor... in an elevator, it's just you, a box, and a cable. It just feels so much more isolating and out of my control. So yeah, it's really just that one specific scenario, nothing else really triggers that feeling of being trapped for me.
Have you ever avoided any other situations or places, even if not elevators, because you were afraid you might panic and not be able to get help or escape easily?

No, honestly, not at all. You mean like... worrying I'll have a panic attack somewhere and be totally stuck? Yeah, no, I don't have that issue anywhere else. It really is just this bizarre, hyper-specific thing with elevators. 

Like, for my job—I do training and development, so I'm often running these big all-day workshops for new hires or flying out to different regional offices to train their staff. So I'm on airplanes fairly often. And if you think about it, an airplane is basically the ultimate "you can't escape" situation, right? You're literally thirty thousand feet in the air in a pressurized metal tube. If you have a panic attack up there, there's no pulling over, there's no stepping outside for some fresh air, you are just stuck until that plane lands. But I actually really love flying! I always try to get the window seat, I just look out at the clouds, or I'll review my training modules on my tablet, and I don't feel even a tiny fraction of anxiety about being trapped or not being able to get a doctor if I needed one. 

And it's the same thing if I'm way out in the middle of nowhere. Like I mentioned camping earlier—sometimes my dad and I would hike miles and miles away from the nearest road, zero cell service, totally off the grid. If something happened out there, we were entirely on our own, miles from any kind of help. But I never once worried about panicking out there. I actually find that kind of isolation super relaxing. 

I don't structure my life around avoiding being trapped. I don't have to sit near the exits at restaurants, I don't avoid driving over long bridges, I don't worry about getting stuck on a Ferris wheel or anything like that. I just live my life completely normally, doing whatever I want to do. I don't even think about the possibility of panicking unless I'm standing in a lobby, staring at those elevator doors. So, yeah, I definitely don't avoid any other places or situations.
